chapter: The Paradise and life in Queens
title: New York's six-month grace period and strict union enforcement
summary: He explains the six-month wait for a union card in New York, strict delegates who pulled people off jobs, and that Detroit's union had been more relaxed.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: I was curious about one thing you mentioned before. When you first came back to New York from Boston, you said you had to wait out a period of time, because of the union.

Well you can't take a steady job in New York at that time unless you ..you have to wait a six month grace period, you know. So, in other words, in that period of time you have...you don't have no money. You can take single engagements, but you can't take no steady job. You can't get no union card until after six months. They give you a temporary card at that time.
What I wanted to ask was about your history in the union: when you first joined the union, when you first became aware of the union, what...
Well I knew when I got

there, I couldn't go on no job. Things were very strict then. If you didn't have a card and there was a union delegate there, checkin' your cards and what not. If you had a temporary card they were very strict and they pulled people off jobs and things like that. So I knew, you know, that you had to have that.
And this was different, this was New York. This was a thing about New York that hadn't happened to you in Detroit or...
No, no, no. No. Uhuh. I joined the union in Detroit but it wasn't like the New York union, you know...Things was a little more relaxed there, you know. But here it was strict.
People did come around and check...
Oh yeah! and raise hell! You know, if your cards weren't right or if your dues weren't paid. Yeah.
